promo-cut-refused.title: Why Cricut refuses your Canva SVG #shorts
promo-cut-refused.description:
Cricut's help pages list what an SVG may not contain: pattern fills, clipping paths, editable text, linked images. A clipping path is their term for one shape masking another — which is exactly what every Canva frame is, and every photo you have dropped into a shape.

So you export, you upload, and Design Space says "Your file includes unsupported items." That is the entire message. It does not say which item and it does not highlight anything.

The culprit here is the photo in the circle. Replace it with a flat colour, export again, and the same design goes straight in — and comes in as separate layers.

When Design Space refuses a Canva file, look for a frame or a photo first. It is almost always that.

promo-cut-vector.title: Not every Canva element is a vector #shorts
promo-cut-vector.description:
Canva mixes true vector elements and raster ones in the same search results — the same way it mixes free and Pro — and it does not label them either way. There is no filter for it.

So test it yourself before you build anything around it. Drop the element on the canvas and scale it up enormously, four or five times the page. A vector stays perfectly crisp at any size. A raster goes soft, then blocky, and you will see it immediately.

Generally the flat single-colour shapes and line icons are vectors. Anything photographic, anything with a soft shadow baked in, anything that looks painted or textured, is not.

Two seconds per element, before you spend twenty minutes composing with something that will never cut.

promo-cut-paths.title: Your SVG stops at 5,000 paths #shorts
promo-cut-paths.description:
Cricut's help pages state that SVGs are restricted to five thousand paths, and more than five thousand causes an upload error.

A path is roughly one outline. A simple icon might be three. A word in a script font is one per letter. A detailed mandala, a leafy wreath, a distressed texture, a halftone pattern — those run to thousands very quickly, and a texture overlay on its own can blow the whole budget.

You cannot see the count in Canva. What you can do is notice when a design is getting busy and ask whether the detail is going to survive being cut anyway.

It usually is not. A shape two millimetres across does not cut, it tears. The path limit and the physical limit tend to arrive together.

promo-cut-weld.title: Canva outlines your text, then it cuts through every join #shorts
promo-cut-weld.description:
Cricut will not accept editable text in an SVG — it has to be shapes. Canva handles that for you automatically, converting text to outlines on export.

But outlining turns every letter into its own separate closed shape. Use a script font where the letters touch and every one of those overlaps is now a cut line running straight through the join. You get your word in pieces.

The fix is Cricut's own tool, not Canva's: select the letters in Design Space and Weld. In their words, it joins shapes by removing any overlapping cut lines — wherever cut paths have intersected, only the exterior cut path remains.

And note this first: once a project has been welded and saved, it cannot be unwelded. Duplicate before you weld.
